question: To meet the ever-increasing demand for poultry products, the agri-food industry uses genetic engineering practices (notably for the Ross 308 strain) to maximise their capacity to produce chickens for commercial purposes. This, alongside poor farming conditions, raises major concerns about animal welfare and the quality of products consumed.

The strain in question, engineered to boost the growth and yield of chickens, adversely affects the poultry – the extreme genetic selection leads to the chickens having physiological deformations and suffering movement and health issues. These sentient beings are reduced to simple products and subjected to physiological stress exceeding their natural capacity, all in the name of profit. In view of the above: 1.
Will the Commission ban the production of genetically modified chickens in Europe?
Will it ban the import of genetically modified chickens in Europe?
More generally, what mechanisms will it put in place to improve animal farming conditions throughout Europe?
answer: In the EU, only genetically modified organisms (GMOs) that have been granted an authorisation can be placed on the market. To obtain such an authorisation, the GMO must undergo a risk assessment according to the provisions laid down in Directive 2001/18/EC (1) and Regulation (EC) No 1829/2003 (2). The risk assessment covers the impact on human and animal health (including animal welfare) and on the environment.

So far, no genetically modified (GM) animals have been authorised in the EU, nor have any applications for authorisation of GM animals been received. Therefore, the placing on the market in the EU of GM chicken, as long as no authorisation has been granted, is prohibited.

The rules for the placing on the market of GMOs in Directive 2001/18/EC and Regulation (EC) No 1829/2003 apply equally to products produced in the EU and imported products. Accordingly, no GM chicken can be imported into the EU as no authorisation for their placing on the market has been granted.

The EU animal welfare legislation provides requirements for the protection of animals at farm (3) and in particular for broilers (4). Enforcement of the EU legislation remains a priority for the Commission who performs regular controls to verify compliance with animal welfare requirements by Member States.
In December 2023, the Commission adopted a proposal for a regulation on the protection of animals during transport.

In the ongoing preparatory work for the revision of the EU animal welfare legislation at farm and at the time of killing the Commission will consider the European Food Safety Authority relevant recommendations including for broilers (5) and the assessment of economic, social, environmental and animal welfare impacts of envisaged measures.

Directive 2001/18/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 12 March 2001 on the deliberate release into the environment of genetically modified organisms and repealing Council Directive 90/220/EEC (OJ L 106, 17.4.2001, p. 1). Regulation (EC) No 1829/2003 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 22 September 2003 on genetically modified food and feed (OJ L 268, 18.10.2003, p. 1-23).
